title: Are sanctions really an alternative to war?
subtitle: Iraq under embargo
subject: comprendreLeMonde
description: In 1990, the UN cut Iraq off from world trade to make Saddam Hussein back down without firing a shot. Ten years later, raw sewage was pouring into the rivers and hospitals were losing their doctors.
author: mark-n-hoffman

hero.hook: An embargo does not fire a single shot. In Iraq, it still made the water dangerous to drink.

blocks.text: To make a government back down without sending in the army, there is a weapon: [[economic sanctions]]. Ban its oil sales, freeze its assets, block its purchases of machinery, including the equipment that treats water. In **2015**, Barack Obama argued that this kind of pressure had brought Iran to the negotiating table: Tehran limited its nuclear program in return for sanctions relief.

How does the pressure work? A targeted government may give in to regain access to its funds. But the effects quickly spill beyond the leaders: ordinary people can no longer afford food or find medicine, and water systems break down for lack of spare parts. Iraq in the **1990s** lived through exactly that.

The UN Charter keeps the two registers apart. Article 41 authorizes measures "not involving the use of armed force," such as cutting economic relations. Article 42 allows military action if those measures prove inadequate. That is why sanctions are so often presented as an alternative to war.

Sanctions work through rules imposed on banks and businesses: no payments to the targeted government, no sales of machinery to it. When the [[UN Security Council]] adopts them, every member state has to enforce them. The promise of lifting them is the bait: the targeted government knows what it stands to gain by giving in.

blocks.caption: Kuwaiti oil wells burning in 1991: the war drove Iraq out of Kuwait, but the embargo stayed in place.

blocks.text: In August **1990**, after Iraq invaded Kuwait, the Council banned almost all trade with Baghdad. Cut off from its oil sales, the regime of [[Saddam Hussein]] lost its revenue: its opponents hoped to force it to withdraw. Iraqi troops were driven out in the **1991** [[Gulf War]], but the embargo remained. Lifting it was now conditional on the elimination of Iraq's weapons of mass destruction.
Yet Iraq lived on its oil: oil paid for imported food and basic necessities. Less revenue meant less money to feed the population and keep essential public services running.

sections.title: When clean water is at stake

blocks.text: The war had damaged the power stations and water systems. Repairing them required imported equipment, but the UN sanctions committee held up approval for some of those purchases. In **2000**, the UN secretary-general himself urged the committee to release water and sanitation equipment so that the repairs could go ahead.

blocks.caption: A water treatment plant in Iraq: without imported parts, repairs had to wait.

blocks.text: That same year, the UN estimated that nearly **90%** of the raw sewage from Iraq's pumping stations was flowing straight into rivers and streams. People who depended on that water were exposed to disease. Repairs were already difficult, with little money and few trained staff. On top of that, sanctions delayed the equipment that would have got the plants working: they acted as another mechanism of violent coercion, not as its alternative.

As the economy collapsed, families struggled to feed themselves. Oil revenue had also paid public salaries: poorly paid doctors and teachers changed jobs or left the country, and hospitals and schools ran short of staff. The UN reported that most Iraqis were struggling to survive. A few wealthy people close to power kept their standard of living, and the gap widened.

blocks.caption: Ration distribution under the Oil-for-Food Programme, late 1990s.

blocks.text: In **1995**, the [[Oil-for-Food Programme]] allowed Iraq to sell oil, under UN supervision, to buy food, medicine and civilian supplies. Shortages eased, but a humanitarian program is no substitute for a working economy. A UN panel even found that dependence on rations had tightened the government's grip on people's lives. Iraqis came out poorer and more dependent on the very regime being targeted.

The Iraqi crisis changed the way sanctions are imposed. After the revelations about the damage they had done, the Security Council turned to narrower measures, asset freezes, travel bans, arms restrictions, aimed at specific leaders while sparing the population. Since **2004**, UN sanctions regimes have followed this so-called targeted approach.

Many families who survived the bombing of 1991 later fell seriously ill from drinking contaminated water. Sanctions had delayed the equipment that would have made it safe. They inflicted physical harm on civilians, even as they were defended as a nonviolent alternative to war.

blocks.text: The choice between "sanctions or war" itself does violence to our ability to think. If those are the only two thinkable options, evidence that both harm civilians is used to pick the lesser evil, not to rethink the options. This is what is called [[structural violence]]: it sets the terms of the debate in advance and rules out some responses before they are even examined. Policies that leave people hungry or sick then look necessary.
Presented as a peaceful alternative to war, the sanctions on Iraq made the water dangerous and emptied the hospitals: another form of violence, and one that fell mostly on civilians.
